questions.question: To test whether a basic solution of an equality-form LP is feasible, some variables are first set to zero and the equations are solved for the others. Which values must then be checked for nonnegativity?
options: The solved values; the zeroed variables pass automatically
The zeroed values; the solved values satisfy the equations
Only the solved original decision variables, not the slacks
Every equation once more, since solving may have broken it

questions.question: The LP with $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has equality form $x_1+2x_2+s_1=8$, $3x_1+x_2+s_2=9$ with all four variables required to be $\ge0$. Setting $x_2=s_2=0$ and solving, what is $(x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)$?

The LP with $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has equality form $x_1+2x_2+s_1=8$, $3x_1+x_2+s_2=9$ with all four variables required to be $\ge0$. Setting $x_1=s_2=0$ gives $(x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(0,9,-10,0)$. How is this point classified?
options: Basic feasible, since $x_1,x_2\ge0$
Not basic, since one value is negative
Feasible but not basic, since $s_2=0$
Basic but infeasible, since $s_1<0$

questions.question: Giapetto's LP in equality form is $2x_s+x_t+s_1=100$, $x_s+x_t+s_2=80$, $x_s+s_3=40$, with all five variables required to be $\ge0$. Which point $(x_s,x_t)$, with its slacks computed, is a basic feasible solution?
An equality-form LP has $m$ equations in $n$ variables. A basic solution sets $n-m$ variables to zero and solves uniquely for the rest. Why can it have only finitely many basic feasible solutions?
options: Each one is fixed by which $n-m$ variables are chosen as zero
Each one is a feasible point, and feasible regions are finite
Each one has integer values, as the equation data are integer
Each one has a different objective value from all the others

questions.question: Giapetto's LP in equality form is $2x_s+x_t+s_1=100$, $x_s+x_t+s_2=80$, $x_s+s_3=40$, with all five variables required to be $\ge0$. With profit $z=3x_s+2x_t$ to maximize, which basic solution gives the best feasible plan?

The LP with $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has equality form $x_1+2x_2+s_1=8$, $3x_1+x_2+s_2=9$ with all four variables required to be $\ge0$. If the right-hand side $8$ is raised to $20$, how many basic feasible solutions does the new LP have?
options: 4, since the same choices of zero variables remain feasible
3, since the constraint lines now meet outside the region
4, since $(0,9)$ joins and $(2,3)$ remains a corner point
6, since every choice of two zero variables is now feasible

questions.question: An LP is written in equality form with slack variables. A basic solution sets some variables to zero and solves the equations uniquely for the rest. Which condition holds exactly when a basic solution is a basic feasible solution?
options: All its original decision variables are nonnegative
All its variables, slacks included, are nonnegative
All its solved-for variables are strictly positive
It gives the best objective value among basic ones

questions.question: The LP with $x_1+2x_2\le8$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ has equality form $x_1+2x_2+s_1=8$, $3x_1+x_2+s_2=9$ with all four variables required to be $\ge0$. (A basic solution sets $n-m$ of the $n$ variables to zero and solves the $m$ equations uniquely for the rest.) How many basic feasible solutions are there?
For an LP in equality form with all variables required to be $\ge0$, how are basic feasible solutions related to feasible solutions?
options: Every feasible solution is a BFS, but not every BFS is feasible
BFS and feasible solutions are always the same set of points
A BFS need not be feasible, as it may have a negative slack
Every BFS is feasible; a feasible solution need not be basic

questions.question: An LP has constraints $\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i$ with every $b_i\ge0$, slacks $s_i$, and all variables required to be $\ge0$. Why is the point $x=0$, $s=b$ then a basic feasible solution?
options: Setting all $x_j=0$ always satisfies every objective function
Setting every $x_j=0$ leaves $s_i=b_i$, which are all $\ge0$
Slacks are nonnegative by definition, whatever the $x_j$ are
A point with only zero decision variables is never infeasible

questions.question: Giapetto's LP in equality form is $2x_s+x_t+s_1=100$, $x_s+x_t+s_2=80$, $x_s+s_3=40$, with all five variables required to be $\ge0$. Which two variables are zero at the corner $(x_s,x_t)=(40,20)$?
options: $x_t$ and $s_3$

questions.question: A feasible LP in equality form, with all variables nonnegative, has a finite optimum. A known result says that some optimal solution is then a basic feasible solution. Combined with the corner-point view, what does this justify?
options: Every BFS of the LP is also an optimal solution of the LP
Every optimal solution of the LP must itself be a BFS
Checking the finitely many BFS is enough to find an optimum
Basic infeasible solutions may also be optimal solutions

questions.question: Giapetto's LP in equality form is $2x_s+x_t+s_1=100$, $x_s+x_t+s_2=80$, $x_s+s_3=40$, with all five variables required to be $\ge0$. A new limit $x_t+s_4=50$ ($x_t\le50$, $s_4\ge0$) is added. With $s_1=s_2=0$ the enlarged system still gives $(x_s,x_t)=(20,60)$. What is it now?
options: Still a BFS, because $s_1$ and $s_2$ stay zero
Still basic, but now infeasible because $s_4=-10$
No longer basic, as three zeros are now needed
Still feasible, because $x_s$ and $x_t$ are $\ge0$
